overview: Styracosaurus albertensis ("spiked lizard") was a centrosaurine ceratopsid from the Campanian of Alberta (~75 Ma), bearing one of the most elaborate frill and horn arrays of any ceratopsian: a large nasal horn up to 60 cm long, four to six long curved spikes projecting from the frill margin, and smaller frill ornaments. Its elaborate display structures make it one of the most recognisable ceratopsids.

Bone beds in the Dinosaur Park Formation preserve dozens of Styracosaurus individuals together — one of the best-documented centrosaurine bone beds. These mass-death assemblages are interpreted as herd drownings during river crossings, analogous to modern wildebeest migrations, and provide population-level data on growth rates, health and demographics.

articles.title: Discovery and horn array
articles.body: Named by Lambe in 1913 from Alberta material. The nasal horn is the primary weapon; the frill spikes are too slender and curved for combat and functioned as display structures. Different individuals show variation in frill spike number and curvature — probably individual variation, age variation or mild sexual dimorphism. A second species, S. ovatus from the Two Medicine Formation of Montana, has a different frill spike arrangement.

articles.title: Bone beds and herding
articles.body: Centrosaurine bone beds — where dozens to thousands of individuals accumulated together — are a characteristic feature of the Dinosaur Park Formation. The leading hypothesis is catastrophic mass mortality during seasonal migrations: herds attempting to cross flooded rivers were swept away and deposited as bone concentrations on the downstream side. The demographic profiles of Styracosaurus bone beds are consistent with a mixed-age herd.

articles.title: Frill function
articles.body: The elaborate frill ornamentation of Styracosaurus — multiple long curved spikes plus smaller accessory ornaments — is disproportionate to any purely defensive function. Sexual selection for increasingly elaborate display structures is the most widely supported hypothesis: the frill acted as a billboard for species recognition and mate quality assessment, analogous to peacock tail feathers or deer antlers.

facts: Its long nasal horn and frill spikes are directly preserved but vary among individuals.
Rubeosaurus ovatus has been proposed as a second Styracosaurus species, a synonymy that remains debated.

presentation.heroLead: A spike-frilled horned dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, documented by several skulls, two partial skeletons and a bonebed, whose wildly variable frill spikes are at the centre of a debate over species and individual variation.

animalParagraphs: Styracosaurus was a rhinoceros-sized horned dinosaur that lived on the coastal plains of what is now southern Alberta about 76 to 75 million years ago. It was around five metres long and walked on four sturdy legs, with a deep beaked skull carrying a single long nasal horn and a frill fringed with four to six long spikes.

The nasal horn could exceed half a metre in length, while the brow horns were reduced to low bumps. The frill spikes are the animal's signature, but they vary strikingly between individuals in number, length and curvature, and one skull even has a small extra spike growing from the middle of the frill. This variation is real, not reconstruction, and complicates attempts to name species from frill shape alone.

Its jaws held batteries of shearing teeth for processing tough vegetation, and it belonged to Centrosaurinae, the short-frilled branch of the horned dinosaurs. Bonebeds containing many individuals show that at least some centrosaurines lived or died in groups, although Styracosaurus itself is known from far fewer individuals than Centrosaurus.
animalHighlights: A single nasal horn more than 50 cm long, with the brow horns reduced to small bumps.
A frill edged with four to six long spikes whose number and shape vary from one skull to the next.
Batteries of tightly packed shearing teeth and a deep, parrot-like beak for cropping plants.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by beak and dental batteries
lifeCards.reason: The toothless beak and shearing tooth batteries match a diet of tough, low-growing plants; the specific plants eaten are not preserved.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Robust forelimbs and hindlimbs are known from the holotype skeleton and AMNH 5372; forelimb posture is still modelled rather than observed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is reasonably constrained by two partial skeletons; masses of about two tonnes are estimates.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The bony horn cores and spikes are real, but their keratin sheaths, skin and colour are inferred.

presentation.classificationSummary: Styracosaurus is a centrosaurine ceratopsid, close to Centrosaurus and to the pachyrhinosaurs. Whether the Montana species Rubeosaurus ovatus should be returned to Styracosaurus, as some recent work proposes, remains disputed.

Compare with the long-frilled, three-horned chasmosaurine of the latest Cretaceous.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: Styracosaurus parksi, named from AMNH 5372, is now treated as S. albertensis. Whether Rubeosaurus ovatus from Montana is a second Styracosaurus species remains debated.

questions.title: Why do the frills differ so much?
questions.copy: Spike number and shape vary between skulls and even between the two sides of one skull. Individual variation and growth explain much of it, which makes species defined on ornament alone hard to test.

questions.title: What were the spikes for?
questions.copy: Display and species recognition are the usual interpretations. There is no direct evidence of combat use, and the keratin sheaths that would have covered the spikes are not preserved.

review.ageReviewNote: The species is restricted to late Campanian Dinosaur Park Formation, near 76-75 Ma.

panel.headline: Several skulls, two partial skeletons and a bonebed from Alberta.
panel.standfirst: Styracosaurus albertensis is anchored by the holotype skull collected in 1913, whose lower jaws and much of the skeleton were recovered from the same quarry in 1935. A second skull and skeleton at the American Museum, further skulls and a Dinosaur Park bonebed round out the record.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Skull, vertebral column, girdles and limbs are all represented in more than one individual, including two associated partial skeletons and bonebed material; the frill is known from several skulls.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete and partial skulls with the nasal horn and spiked frill, lower jaws, the vertebral column, ribs, pectoral and pelvic girdles and limb bones of at least two associated individuals, and disarticulated bones from a multi-individual bonebed in Dinosaur Provincial Park.
knownRemains.note: Even with several skulls, the sample is small compared with Centrosaurus, so the full range of frill variation and the growth series are incompletely known.

specimenCards.title: AMNH 5372 · skull and skeleton
specimenCards.description: A skull and partial skeleton collected by Barnum Brown in 1915 and named Styracosaurus parksi in 1937. It is now regarded as S. albertensis and is mounted at the American Museum of Natural History.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Several skulls with horn cores and frill spikes, two associated partial skeletons and bonebed material from one formation.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A centrosaurine plant-eater whose extravagant frill spikes were most likely display structures, with variation reflecting growth and individuals rather than many species.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The function of the horn and spikes, the keratin sheaths, the full growth series, and whether Rubeosaurus ovatus belongs in the genus.
